course.title: Baby First Health Early Childhood Development Certificate

module.title: Physical Development in Early Childhood

target_learners.raw: Parents, caregivers, childcare workers, teachers, health practitioners, and other adults caring for children aged 0–5.
list: Other adults caring for children aged 0–5

learning_objectives: Understand gross and fine motor skills
Use milestones as helpful guides rather than deadlines
Know when to seek professional advice

outline.title: When Should a Parent Be Concerned?
Common Mistakes Parents and Caregivers Make

blocks.text: Welcome to Module 2 of the Baby First Health Early Childhood Development Certificate.

In this module, you will learn what physical development means, how children build movement skills from birth to age five, and how you can safely support a child’s physical abilities through everyday play, nutrition, sleep, and responsive care.

By the end, you should be able to explain physical development, understand gross and fine motor skills, use milestones as helpful guides rather than deadlines, and know when to seek professional advice.
items: Understand gross and fine motor skills
Use milestones as helpful guides rather than deadlines
Know when to seek professional advice

blocks.text: Physical development is the way a child’s body grows and learns to move and use its muscles. It includes growth in height and weight, but it is much more than that.

items.text: Physical growth means changes in the body’s size, such as becoming taller, heavier, or having larger muscles and bones.
Physical development means learning to control and use the body. This includes holding up the head, sitting, walking, running, holding a spoon, drawing, climbing, and balancing.

blocks.title: A simple example
blocks.text: A child may grow taller and gain weight, but physical development is also seen when the child learns to:
items: Pick up a piece of food
Walk without holding an adult’s hand
Turn the pages of a book

blocks.text: Physical development supports a child’s independence. When a child learns to walk, hold objects, dress, eat, and play, they can do more for themselves and take part more fully in family and community life.
Gross motor skills are movements that use the large muscles of the body. These include the arms, legs, back, and trunk—the middle part of the body.

These skills usually develop step by step. A baby first needs head control before sitting well. A child usually needs to walk before running confidently. However, children do not all follow exactly the same order or timing.
For example, one child may walk at 11 months, while another may walk at 15 months. Both can be developing well. What matters most is that the child is making steady progress over time.
Fine motor skills are smaller, more controlled movements, especially of the hands and fingers. They also involve the eyes and hands working together.

items: Picking up small pieces of food

blocks.text: Fine motor skills matter because they help children become more independent. A child who can hold a spoon can try to feed themselves. A child who can hold a crayon can draw and later learn to write. A child who can turn pages can explore books more independently.
Fine motor skills also support learning. When children build, draw, sort, pour, and manipulate objects, they are strengthening hand control, concentration, problem-solving, and coordination.
The ages below are general guides, not deadlines. Children develop at different rates, and many healthy children reach skills earlier or later than others.

Developmental milestones are skills that most children can do by a certain age. The CDC describes milestones as skills that at least 75% of children can do by a given age, which means they are broad population guides rather than exact expectations for every child.

blocks.label: 0–12 months
blocks.summary: During the first year, babies learn to control their bodies and explore the world through movement.
abilities: Lifting the head during tummy time
Sitting with and then without support
Crawling or moving across the floor in their own way
Taking first steps, sometimes around the first birthday

notes.text: Not all babies crawl in the same way. Some crawl forward, some move backward first, and some use other ways to move before walking. The important thing is that the baby is becoming stronger and more mobile over time.

blocks.label: 1–2 years
blocks.summary: Toddlers become more mobile and begin to use their hands for everyday tasks.
abilities: Walking while pulling or carrying a toy
Climbing onto low furniture with supervision

notes.text: At around age two, many children can run, kick a ball, walk up a few stairs with help, and eat with a spoon. These are useful signs of progress, not pass-or-fail tests.

blocks.label: 2–3 years
blocks.summary: Children become more confident movers and begin to coordinate their bodies more smoothly.
abilities: Walking up and down stairs while holding on

notes.text: At this age, children often enjoy active games such as chasing, dancing, carrying objects, and playing with balls. They need safe space and patient adults, not perfect performance.

blocks.label: 3–4 years
blocks.summary: Preschool children develop better balance, strength, and hand control.
abilities: Hopping or standing briefly on one foot
Using a spoon and fork more confidently

notes.text: By age four, many children can hop, stand on one foot briefly, catch a bounced ball most of the time, and begin to use child-safe scissors with supervision. Again, children vary, and practice matters.

blocks.label: 4–5 years
blocks.summary: Children become more coordinated and independent.
abilities: Beginning to manage clothing, such as buttons or zips

notes.text: By age five, many children can stand on one foot for several seconds, hop, swing, climb, and use a fork and spoon. These abilities prepare children for school activities, games, and greater independence.

blocks.text: Children develop physical skills through opportunity, practice, safety, good health, and encouragement. Adults do not need to “train” children like athletes. Children learn best through play and everyday activities.

blocks.title: Safe opportunities to move and explore

blocks.text: Children need room to move. A baby needs a clean, safe floor space to stretch, roll, reach, and practise tummy time. A toddler needs space to walk, push, carry, and climb safely.
Instead of keeping a toddler seated for long periods, create a safe area where the child can walk, push a small basket, carry plastic cups, or climb a low, stable step with an adult nearby.
WHO recommends that infants be active several times a day through interactive floor-based play, including tummy time for babies who are not yet mobile.
Tummy time means placing an awake baby on their tummy for short periods while an adult watches closely. It helps babies build neck, shoulder, arm, and back strength.
Place a baby on a clean mat on their tummy for a few minutes while awake. Put a safe toy in front of the baby and talk or sing to encourage them to lift their head.
Never leave a baby alone during tummy time. Babies should always sleep on their back in a safe sleep space.
Active play helps children practise movement naturally. It can include dancing, chasing bubbles, playing ball, walking, climbing, pulling toys, or helping with simple household tasks.
A caregiver can put on music and invite a toddler to dance, march, jump, or copy simple movements.

Outdoor play gives children space to run, climb, balance, and explore. It also supports health and wellbeing. WHO notes that regular physical activity and active play are vital for young children’s healthy growth and development.
Outdoor play must always be adapted to the local environment. In hot weather, choose cooler times of day, provide shade and water, and watch for unsafe ground, traffic, animals, or sharp objects.
Children do not need expensive toys. Safe, simple, locally available materials can support movement and hand skills.

items: Spoons and bowls for pretend cooking
Safe household objects for sorting and carrying

blocks.text: A toddler can practise fine motor skills by putting bottle caps into a container, stacking cups, or turning pages of a picture book with an adult.
Skills improve with repetition. Let children try again, even when they spill, fall safely, or do something messily.
If a child is learning to use a spoon, allow practice at mealtimes even if some food falls. Praise the effort: “You are holding your spoon. Well done.”

Children need enough energy and nutrients to grow, move, and stay active. Breastfeeding, appropriate complementary foods from around six months, varied family foods, and enough water support growth and activity. Nutrition is covered in more detail elsewhere in the program.

Sleep allows the body to rest, recover, and grow. WHO recommends about 12–16 hours of sleep in 24 hours for infants aged 4–11 months, 11–14 hours for children aged 1–2 years, and 10–13 hours for children aged 3–4 years, including naps where appropriate.

blocks.title: WHO recommended sleep in 24 hours, including naps where appropriate

blocks.text: Encouraging movement does not mean allowing danger. Remove sharp objects, cover or block unsafe areas, supervise water and climbing, and ensure outdoor spaces are safe.
Routine health visits help monitor growth, nutrition, immunisation, and development. They are also a good time for parents to ask questions about movement, feeding, sleep, or any concern.

Children need time outside of prams, high chairs, car seats, and carriers. WHO advises that infants and children aged 1–2 years should not be restrained for more than one hour at a time, and that young children should not sit for extended periods.
During a long journey, plan safe breaks where a toddler can stretch, walk, and move before returning to the car seat.
Nutrition, sleep, and general health work together to support physical development.

items.label: Nutrition
items.text: Nutrition provides energy for movement and nutrients for bones, muscles, and the brain.

items.label: Sleep
items.text: Sleep helps the body recover and supports growth, attention, mood, and learning.

items.label: General health
items.text: General health affects how well a child can play and learn. Repeated illness, untreated pain, poor vision, or ongoing feeding problems can affect a child’s activity and development.

blocks.text: A child who is well fed, rested, and healthy is usually more able to explore, play, and practise new skills. If a child is often tired, has poor appetite, is not growing as expected, or seems unusually weak or inactive, a qualified healthcare professional should assess the child.
Play is one of the most powerful ways children develop physically. Through play, children practise balance, strength, coordination, problem-solving, and confidence.

WHO describes play as voluntary, enjoyable activity that can be solitary or social and may involve objects. Young children build and strengthen developmental skills through playful interaction with people and objects.

blocks.summary: Babies learn through safe floor movement, reaching, grasping, kicking, rolling, and tummy time.
examples: Place a safe toy just within reach.
Let the baby kick a soft ball.
Talk and sing during tummy time.
Offer safe objects to hold and explore.

blocks.summary: Toddlers need chances to walk, carry, push, pull, climb safely, and practise hand skills.
examples: Let the child carry a small plastic cup to the table.
Provide a ball for rolling or kicking.
Encourage safe climbing on low steps with supervision.
Offer crayons and paper for scribbling.

blocks.summary: Preschool children benefit from running, jumping, balancing, throwing, catching, dancing, and active games.
examples: Play “stop and go” or simple chasing games.
Throw and catch a soft ball.
Walk on a low, safe line drawn on the ground to practise balance.

blocks.text: Children do not need costly equipment. A ball, cups, safe containers, paper, crayons, music, and a safe outdoor space can provide many learning opportunities.
Children develop at different rates. Some walk early. Some talk early. Some become confident climbers later. Some children prefer watching before they try a new movement.
This variation is normal. A child should not be constantly compared with a sibling, cousin, neighbour’s child, or classmate.

However, “children develop differently” should never be used to dismiss a real concern. A caregiver knows the child well. If a child is not progressing, has persistent difficulty with movement, or loses a skill they previously had, it is important to speak with a qualified healthcare professional.
The CDC advises parents to act early if a child is not meeting milestones, has lost skills, or if the parent has any concern.

lessons.title: When Should a Parent Be Concerned?

blocks.text: A developmental concern does not automatically mean something is wrong, but it is worth discussing with a qualified professional.

blocks.intro: Speak with a doctor, nurse, or other qualified child-health professional if you notice:
items: The child is not making expected progress in movement over time.
The child has significant difficulty with movement compared with their usual abilities.
The child persistently uses one side of the body much more than the other.
The child loses a skill they previously had, such as no longer walking or sitting as before.
The child has major difficulty with walking, balance, coordination, or using their hands.
The child seems unusually stiff, floppy, weak, or in pain during movement.
The parent or caregiver has a concern that continues or seems unusual.

blocks.text: The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends ongoing developmental monitoring and standardized developmental screening at set ages, with additional assessment whenever parents or professionals have concerns.

Do not try to diagnose a child using the internet. A single late skill does not automatically mean a disorder. What matters is the overall pattern of the child’s development, whether progress is continuing, and whether skills are being lost.

blocks.title: Case: Amara and her two-year-old son, Musa

narrative.text: Amara lives in a busy neighbourhood in Yaoundé. Her son, Musa, is two years old. At a family gathering, Amara notices that her sister’s child, who is also two, runs confidently and kicks a ball. Musa walks well but prefers to hold his mother’s hand and does not run much.
Amara becomes worried. A neighbour tells her that Musa must be “delayed” because he is not running like the other child.

narrative.intro: Amara decides to observe Musa calmly for one week. She notices that he:
items: Walks steadily and climbs onto the sofa with help
Picks up small objects and puts them into a bowl
Holds a spoon and tries to feed himself
Kicks a ball when it is placed close to him
Is learning new words and follows simple instructions

narrative.text: Amara also creates more chances for movement. She lets Musa carry safe plastic cups to the table, kick a ball in a safe open space, and scribble with crayons. She reduces long periods when he is seated or restrained.

After two weeks, Musa is beginning to take a few quick running steps when playing chase with his mother. Amara still decides to mention her earlier concern at Musa’s next health visit, especially because she wants reassurance and professional guidance.

what_this_case_teaches.heading: What this case teaches
items: Children should not be judged only by comparison with another child.
It is helpful to observe the child’s overall abilities, not one skill alone.
Children need safe daily opportunities to move and practise.
A caregiver’s concern deserves respectful attention.
If a concern continues, a qualified healthcare professional should assess the child.

items.question: Why was it helpful for Amara to observe Musa over several days instead of deciding immediately that something was wrong?
What physical skills was Musa already showing?
What simple, low-cost activities could Amara use to encourage Musa’s movement?
When should Amara seek professional advice about Musa’s physical development?
How can caregivers support a child without comparing them with other children?

lessons.title: Common Mistakes Parents and Caregivers Make

blocks.title: Observation activity: “Watch, Support, Encourage”
blocks.instructions: Choose a child aged 0–5 whom you care for. Observe the child during normal, safe play for 10–15 minutes. Do not test, pressure, or diagnose the child.

record_items.examples: crawling, walking, running, climbing, balancing, jumping, or dancing.

record_items.prompt: How the child uses their hands
record_items.examples: reaching, grasping, holding a spoon, turning pages, stacking, drawing, or picking up objects.

record_items.prompt: What physical activities the child enjoys
record_items.examples: ball play, dancing, climbing, carrying objects, drawing, or outdoor play.

record_items.prompt: What skills the child is practising
record_items.examples: balance, coordination, hand control, strength, or independence.

record_items.prompt: How you can safely encourage more movement
record_items.examples: providing floor space, offering a ball, allowing safe climbing, encouraging self-feeding, or reducing long periods of sitting.

blocks.follow_up: After the observation, write down one simple change you can make this week to give the child more safe opportunities to move and play.

items.text: Physical development is more than getting taller and heavier; it includes learning to move and use the body.
Physical growth refers to changes in body size, while physical development includes movement skills and coordination.
Gross motor skills are large-body movements such as sitting, walking, running, jumping, and climbing.
Fine motor skills are smaller hand-and-finger movements such as grasping, feeding, drawing, and turning pages.
Developmental milestones are useful general guides, not exact deadlines.
Children develop at different rates, and progress over time matters more than comparison with other children.
Safe floor play, tummy time, active play, outdoor play, and everyday tasks support physical development.
Good nutrition, adequate sleep, safety, and regular healthcare all support healthy development.
Children do not need expensive toys; safe, simple, locally available materials can support play and learning.
Persistent concerns, significant movement difficulties, or loss of previously learned skills should be discussed with a qualified healthcare professional.

questions.question: What is physical development?

options.text: Only a child’s height and weight
The way a child’s body grows and learns to move and use muscles
Only a child’s ability to read
Only a child’s personality

questions.explanation: Physical development includes growth, movement, coordination, and physical abilities.

questions.question: Which is an example of a gross motor skill?

options.text: Turning a page
Holding a spoon
Running
Scribbling

questions.explanation: Running uses large muscles and is a gross motor skill.

questions.question: Which is an example of a fine motor skill?

options.text: Crawling
Walking
Jumping
Picking up a small object

questions.explanation: Picking up a small object requires controlled hand and finger movements.

questions.question: What should caregivers remember about developmental milestones?

options.text: They are exact deadlines for every child
They are general guides that most children reach by certain ages
They prove whether a child is intelligent
They should replace professional advice

questions.explanation: Milestones are broad guides, not rigid deadlines. Children develop at different rates.

questions.question: A baby is awake and not yet mobile. Which activity helps build strength for later movement?

options.text: Keeping the baby in a car seat for long periods
Supervised tummy time and floor play
Watching television
Avoiding all movement

questions.explanation: WHO recommends interactive floor-based play and tummy time for infants who are not yet mobile.

questions.question: A two-year-old walks well but is not yet running as confidently as another two-year-old. What is the best first response?

options.text: Assume the child has a serious disorder
Punish the child for not running
Observe overall progress, provide safe movement opportunities, and seek advice if concerns continue
Compare the child daily with other children

questions.explanation: Children vary in timing. Caregivers should support practice and seek professional advice if concerns persist or skills are lost.

questions.question: Why are fine motor skills important?

options.text: They help children become more independent in everyday tasks
They replace the need for gross motor skills
They are only important for children who want to become artists
They develop without practice or opportunity

questions.explanation: Fine motor skills support feeding, dressing, drawing, handling objects, and later writing.

questions.question: Which situation should be discussed with a qualified healthcare professional?

options.text: A child walks at 13 months instead of 11 months
A child prefers one game over another
A child loses the ability to walk after previously walking
A child is quieter during illness

questions.explanation: Loss of a previously acquired skill is an important concern that should be assessed promptly.

questions.question: A caregiver wants to support a toddler’s physical development at home. Which is the best approach?

options.text: Buy expensive electronic toys
Keep the child seated to prevent falls
Provide safe space for walking, carrying, climbing, and ball play
Allow unrestricted access to every area of the home

questions.explanation: Children develop through safe, repeated opportunities to move and explore.

questions.question: A parent is worried about a child’s movement but has no other clear concern. What should the parent do?

options.text: Wait silently until the child is much older
Search online and diagnose the child
Share the concern with a qualified healthcare professional and ask about developmental screening if needed
Stop the child from all physical activity

questions.explanation: Parents know their children well. Persistent concerns should be discussed with a qualified professional, who can decide whether screening or referral is needed.

terms.definition: The way a child’s body grows and learns to move, coordinate, and use muscles.
Changes in body size, such as height, weight, and body proportions.
Movements using large muscles, such as sitting, crawling, walking, running, jumping, and climbing.
Smaller, controlled movements, especially of the hands and fingers, such as grasping, feeding oneself, drawing, and turning pages.
A skill that most children can do by a certain age, used as a general guide rather than a strict deadline.
The ability to use different parts of the body smoothly together, such as using the eyes and hands to catch a ball.
Short periods when an awake baby is placed on their tummy while closely supervised, helping build neck, shoulder, and back strength.
A brief, structured check used by qualified professionals to identify children who may need further developmental assessment.

professional_note.title: Professional Note
paragraphs: This module provides educational information about physical development in early childhood. It does not diagnose developmental conditions or replace professional assessment.

Children develop at different rates, and a single difference from a milestone does not automatically mean something is wrong. However, parents and caregivers should seek advice from a qualified healthcare professional when they have ongoing concerns, notice significant movement difficulties, or observe a child losing skills they previously had. Urgent medical concerns should receive appropriate medical attention without delay.
